paragraphs.heading: Expansion in reverse
paragraphs.text: The Big Crunch is a proposed ending for the universe in which expansion one day turns around and everything falls back together. The collapse would go on until the cosmic scale factor reached zero, and it might be followed by a new universe starting with another Big Bang. The idea assumes there is enough matter spread through the universe for gravity to beat the expansion that began with the Big Bang.

paragraphs.heading: Where the idea came from
paragraphs.text: The hypothesis goes back to 1922, when the Russian physicist Alexander Friedmann wrote equations showing that the way the universe ends depends on its density. Rather than staying stable, the universe could either grow or shrink. With enough matter, gravity could stop the expansion and then reverse it. The universe would then fall in on itself, somewhat like a black hole.

paragraphs.heading: The final moments
paragraphs.text: As the collapse went on, the universe would fill with radiation from stars and with high-energy particles. Squeezed together and blueshifted to higher energy, that radiation would become strong enough to set the surfaces of stars burning before the stars crashed together. At the very end the universe would be one huge fireball at a nearly infinite temperature, and then neither time nor space would be left.

paragraphs.heading: What the evidence says
paragraphs.text: Most of the evidence suggests the Big Crunch will not happen. In the late 1990s and early 2000s, distant supernovae used as standard candles, along with detailed maps of the cosmic microwave background, showed that gravity is not slowing the expansion; it is speeding up. The 2011 Nobel Prize in Physics went to researchers who helped make this discovery. That makes a different ending, the Big Chill, more likely. Even so, some physicists think a dark energy fluctuation could cause a crunch-like event, and a 2025 study used a dark-energy model to predict a future Big Crunch.

paragraphs.heading: Einstein's change of mind
paragraphs.text: Albert Einstein favored a universe that did not change. To keep it static, as it seemed to be at the time, he saw that some anti-gravity would be needed to hold back gravity pulling everything together, and this cosmological constant was added to general relativity. Edwin Hubble then paired galaxy distances with redshifts measured by Vesto Slipher and Milton Humason and found that redshift rose roughly in step with distance, proof that the universe was expanding. Einstein dropped the cosmological constant and later called his belief in a static universe his "biggest mistake".

paragraphs.heading: Crunch, bounce, repeat
paragraphs.text: A related idea, the Big Bounce, says that after a crunch the universe could begin expanding again with another Big Bang. If this repeated forever, the result would be a cyclic universe that passes through endless rounds of expansion and contraction. Einstein briefly considered such cycles in 1931. More modern versions exist too, such as Paul Steinhardt's ekpyrotic model, in which the Big Bang may have come from two parallel planes, called branes, colliding in a higher-dimensional space.
